learningObjective: Explain the design intent of Ansor's task scheduler for allocating autotuning budget across subgraphs.

canonicalClaims.claim: Ansor's task scheduler allocates a global autotuning time budget across the subgraphs (tasks) of a full model based on their current measured latency contribution and their estimated marginal improvement, so that time is spent on the subgraphs whose speedups matter most for end-to-end latency rather than distributing budget uniformly.
conditions: End-to-end latency is the objective (not per-task speedup in isolation).
Tasks have differing runtime contributions and differing improvement potentials.
nonImplications: Does not imply that the scheduler ignores per-task quality; it prunes tasks whose marginal improvement is small relative to their share of end-to-end time.
Does not imply that a task with the largest raw latency is always tuned first — a task with small latency but large marginal potential may still receive budget.

canonicalClaims.claim: Uniform-budget baselines (equal time per subgraph) waste tuning effort on subgraphs that already run near-optimally or contribute little to end-to-end time.
conditions: The workload has heterogeneous per-subgraph runtimes.
nonImplications: Does not imply uniform budget is always worst; on very small models it can be competitive.

misconceptions.claim: The Ansor task scheduler distributes budget uniformly across all tasks so that every operator receives the same number of measurements.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The paper argues explicitly against uniform allocation and introduces the scheduler as its remedy.

misconceptions.claim: The task scheduler picks tasks by highest peak speedup measured so far; tasks whose peak has plateaued are dropped immediately.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The scheduler weighs marginal improvement against the task's share of end-to-end latency; plateauing alone does not drop a task if its runtime share is dominant.

misconceptions.claim: The Ansor task scheduler's speedups reported in the paper generalize to any end-to-end deep-learning workload on any hardware; the exact percentages are the community consensus.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The paper's numbers are for specific models on specific GPUs/CPUs; treating them as universal violates the paper-scope discipline.
